title: Three days. Three temptations. Three denials.
paragraphs: Three days. Three temptations. Three denials.
Throughout the Bible, the number three appears at some of the most decisive moments in the story of God’s people.

Not as superstition.
Not as numerology.
But as a pattern of confirmation, testing, and transformation.
Again and again, Scripture shows us that the third moment often reveals the turning point.

Sometimes it reveals weakness.
Sometimes it reveals faith.
Sometimes it reveals the beginning of redemption.
And once you start noticing it, you see it everywhere in the biblical story.
Before Jesus began His public ministry, He was led into the wilderness.
For forty days He fasted.
At His weakest physical moment, Satan came with three temptations (Matthew 4:1–11).

First, he challenged Jesus to turn stones into bread.
Then he tempted Him to throw Himself from the temple.
Finally, he offered the kingdoms of the world.
Three temptations.
Each one attacking something deeper than hunger.

Identity.
Trust.
Authority.
And three times Jesus answered with the same weapon:
“It is written.”
The third temptation did not break Him.
It revealed Him.
Later, on the darkest night of the Gospel story, another set of three moments unfolds.

Peter, the disciple who boldly promised,
“Even if all fall away, I will not” (Mark 14:29).
But in the courtyard of the high priest, fear replaced courage.
A servant girl recognized him.
“You also were with Jesus.”
Peter denied it.
Then someone else asked.
He denied it again.
Then a third voice insisted.
And Peter denied Jesus for the third time.
Immediately the rooster crowed.
Luke tells us something heartbreaking happened next.
“The Lord turned and looked at Peter.” (Luke 22:61)
Three denials.
Three failures.
Three moments Peter wished he could erase.
But God was not finished with Peter.
After the resurrection, Jesus met His disciples by the Sea of Galilee.
Peter had gone back to fishing.
Maybe he believed his failure had disqualified him.
Maybe he thought the story was over.
But Jesus did something remarkable.
Three times He asked Peter a question.
“Simon, son of John, do you love Me?” (John 21:15–17)
Three times.
The same number as the denials.
Not to shame him.
But to restore him.
For every denial, Jesus gave Peter a chance to declare love again.
And after each answer, Jesus gave a command:
“Feed my lambs.”
“Take care of my sheep.”
“Feed my sheep.”
Peter’s worst failure became the doorway to his calling.
Then there are the three days that changed history.
After the crucifixion, Jesus was placed in a tomb.
The stone was sealed.
Roman guards stood watch.
Hope seemed buried.
But Jesus had already told His disciples what would happen.
“The Son of Man must be killed and after three days rise again.” (Mark 8:31)
Three days of silence.
Three days of grief.
Three days when it looked like darkness had won.
But the third day was never meant to be the end.
It was the moment God would rewrite the story.
The stone rolled away.
The tomb was empty.
Death was defeated.
And the world would never be the same.
Even earlier in Scripture, the pattern appears.
Jonah spent three days and three nights in the belly of a great fish before being delivered (Jonah 1:17).
Later, Jesus would say that Jonah’s experience was a sign pointing to His own resurrection (Matthew 12:40).
Paul spent three days blind after encountering Christ on the road to Damascus before receiving sight and stepping into his mission (Acts 9:9–18).
Three days.
Three moments.
Three turning points.
The Bible also establishes an important principle in Deuteronomy 19:15:
“A matter must be established by the testimony of two or three witnesses.”
In other words, truth is confirmed through repetition.
And throughout Scripture, the number three often marks divine confirmation.
A moment God wants people to recognize.
A moment where the heart is revealed.
A moment where a decision becomes unavoidable.
But maybe the most powerful lesson is this:
God often meets us in the third moment.

The third temptation.
The third failure.
The third day.
The moment when we think everything is over.
Peter thought his third denial defined him.
The disciples thought the third day meant defeat.
But God was writing a different ending.
Because in the hands of God, the third moment is often where redemption begins.
Maybe you are in a “second moment” right now.

Still in the struggle.
Still in the silence.
Still in the uncertainty.
But the biblical pattern reminds us of something powerful.
The story is not finished yet.
Because sometimes…
the third moment is where everything changes.

The third prayer.
The third attempt.
The third day.
And suddenly what looked like the end becomes the beginning of something God had planned all along.
Which “three moment” in the Bible has impacted you the most?

Peter’s restoration?
Jesus’ resurrection after three days?
Jonah’s three days in the fish?
Let’s learn from Scripture together.
